newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul to reform labour laws within year - minister.
newsitem.headline: Seoul to reform labour laws within year - minister.

text.p: The South Korean government, faced with growing confrontations between labour and employer groups, plans to revise labour laws within this year, Labour Minister Jin Nyum said on Sunday.

"(We) agreed to recommend the president draw up the government's own draft bill and send it to the National Assembly on an early date," Jin said after a meeting of senior officials from the government and the ruling party.
Prime Minister Lee Soo-sung presided over the meeting, in which cabinet ministers and senior New Korea Party officials participated, an official at the Prime Minister's Office said.
Earlier, a presidential advisory commission, formed after President Kim Young-sam pledged in late April to reform labour laws, failed to draw up a compromise draft bill.
But Jin did not say what the government's position would be in settling confrontations on key issues between labour and employer groups.

Key issues at stake include the abolishment of articles that ban outside intervention in labour disputes, restrict the number of unions in each workplace, bar unionists from taking part in political activities and ban public servants and teachers from forming labour unions.
Sunday's report came just several hours before the Korea Confederation of Trade Unions (KCTU) was to start a massive rally in Seoul to press for a sweeping reform of labour laws.
The KCTU, the nation's largest independent union grouping said in a newspaper advertisement on Sunday that the government "should hurry up for democratic revisions of labour-related laws."

Last week, two Geneva-based union federations accused Seoul of back off commitments to reform labour laws, and warned they would work to stop South Korea's admission to the Paris-based OECD unless the reform went ahead.
The two groups -- the white-collar workers' federation FIET and the International Metalworkers' Federation -- represent 30 million private service sector workers and metalworkers around the world.
The Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) voted in early October to invite South Korea as the 29th member of the club of industrialised nations.

OECD members -- until now mainly Western industrial powers -- have urged the reform of South Korea's restrictive labour laws, a legacy of the military regimes that ruled the country for decades, to ease its entry.
